cards.front: Why can a final instance field be assigned inside a constructor?
cards.back: Because a constructor runs exactly once per object, and each object has its own copy of the field
cards.extra: The rule is "assigned once per instance", and one constructor call per instance satisfies it. The compiler enforces definite assignment on every path through every constructor.
cards.source: stackoverflow.com — Why can a final instance field be assigned in a constructor but a static final cannot?
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::10 Final Keyword

cards.front: Why is assigning a static final field in a constructor a compile error?
cards.back: A static field is assigned once per class, but the constructor runs once per object — a second object would assign it again
cards.extra: The compiler does not try to prove you create only one object; it rejects the category outright. Static finals belong in a static initializer or at the declaration.
cards.source: stackoverflow.com — Why can a final instance field be assigned in a constructor but a static final cannot?

cards.back: A final field declared without an initializer, which must be definitely assigned by the end of every constructor
cards.extra: private final List foo; is legal only if all constructors assign it exactly once. The compiler tracks this path by path.

cards.front: What does final on a reference variable actually forbid?
cards.back: Reassigning the variable — not modifying the object it points to
cards.extra: foo.add("bar") mutates the list and is fine. Only foo = new ArrayList() is rejected, because that is a second assignment to the variable.

cards.front: Is final a runtime or a compile-time guarantee?
cards.back: Primarily compile-time — the compiler enforces definite single assignment
cards.extra: At runtime the JVM also treats final fields specially (they are frozen at the end of the constructor), but reflection with setAccessible(true) can still write to them.
cards.source: stackoverflow.com — Why can a final instance field be assigned in a constructor but a static final cannot?

cards.front: Why is the instance-field case legal even though the constructor could be called many times?
cards.back: Because "many times" means many objects, and the final field is a different variable in each of them
cards.extra: The static case differs because there is only one variable shared by all objects — so the same prohibition bites.
